title.en: The Sun and Moon Marry: Stones and Birds
title.zh: 日月成婚：石化為男、鳥化為女

region.en: Baining country, Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島拜寧人之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The Baining say that at first only the sun and moon existed; they married, and from their union were born stones and birds — the stones turning into men, the birds into women, from whom the Baining are descended.
summary.zh: 拜寧人之說：太初唯有日月；日月成婚，生出石頭與鳥——石化為男人，鳥化為女人，拜寧人即由此傳下。

passages.text: An origin of man from stone is told by the Baining of New Britain. At first the only beings in the world were the sun and the moon, but they married, and from their union were born stones and birds, the former subsequently turning into men, the latter into women, and from these the Baining are descended. The first ancestors were thus children of the two great lights, solid as the stones of the mountains and swift as the birds of the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tiny Sea in the Tapa-Cloth Cover

region.en: Baining country, Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島拜寧人之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The sea began as a tiny water-hole under a tapa cloth, owned by an old woman for flavouring food. Her sons tore the cover open, and the water spread until it became the sea; the old woman planted twigs along the shore to stop the ocean from destroying all things.
summary.zh: 太初之海僅為老嫗藏於樹皮布下的一小水窪，供她取鹹水調味。二子偷窺後撕開覆布，水洞愈撕愈大，二人攜布角奔逃，水漫成海，幾滅萬物；老嫗急植樹枝於岸邊，方遏止海洋。

passages.text: In the beginning the sea was very small — only a tiny water-hole, belonging to an old woman, from which she got the salt water for the flavouring of her food. She kept the hole concealed under a cover of tapa cloth, and though her two sons repeatedly asked her whence she obtained the salt water, she refused to answer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they determined to watch, and eventually surprised her in the act of lifting the cover and dipping up the salt water. When she had gone they went to the spot and tore the cover open; and the farther they tore, the larger became the water-hole. Terrified by this, they ran away, each carrying a corner of the cloth; and thus the water spread and spread until it became the sea, which rose so that only a few rocks, covered with earth, remained above it. When the old woman saw that the sea constantly grew larger, she feared that the entire world would be covered by it, so she hastily planted some twigs along the edge of the shore, thus preventing the ocean from destroying all things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Mushrooms Thrown to the Sky

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: When the sea had dried and the first two beings had planted trees and made food, they made two mushrooms: the man threw one into the sky to create the moon, the woman tossed the other upward and formed the sun.
summary.zh: 海水退去、初民種樹造食之後，首二人又造二菇：男將一菇擲入天空，化為月亮；女將另一菇拋上去，化為太陽。

passages.text: In the Admiralty Islands it is said that when the sea had dried so that man appeared, the first two beings, after planting trees and creating food plants, made two mushrooms, one of which the man threw into the sky, creating the moon, while the woman tossed the other upward and formed the sun. Thus the two lights of the world were the work of the first couple's hands, flung up from their garden on the new land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon Dug Up Too Soon

region.en: Port Moresby district, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞莫爾茲比港一帶（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A man digging a deep hole uncovered the moon as a small bright object. It grew in his hands, escaped, and rose into the sky — but because it was taken out prematurely, it sheds only feeble rays instead of the brighter light it would have given had it been left to be born naturally.
summary.zh: 有人掘深坑時掘出一小小發亮之物——月亮。月亮在他手中漸漸長大，掙脫而出，升上天空；惟因早產而出，其光微弱，未能如自然誕生時那般明亮。

passages.text: A different account of the moon is given by the people of southern British New Guinea. A man was digging a deep hole one day when he uncovered the moon as a small bright object. After he had taken it out, it began to grow, and finally, escaping from his hands, rose high into the sky. Had the moon been left in the ground until it was born naturally, it would have given a brighter light; but since it was taken out prematurely, it sheds only feeble rays — the dim moonlight of every night since bearing the mark of that man's impatience.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

region.en: German New Guinea coast (symbolic pin: Huon Gulf)
region.zh: 德屬新幾內亞海岸（象徵定位：休恩灣）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The moon was kept hidden in a jar by an old woman until boys discovered and opened it; the moon flew out and rose into the sky, bearing the marks of their hands on its surface.
summary.zh: 太初月亮藏於一老嫗之罐中。幾個男孩偷開罐口，月亮飛出，掙脫他們的手，升上天空——月面上至今仍留著他們的指印。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); New Guinea coast heritage.

passages.text: A tale from German New Guinea recounts how the moon was originally kept hidden in a jar by an old woman. Some boys discovered this, and coming secretly, opened the jar, whereupon the moon flew out; and though they tried to hold it, it slipped from their grasp and rose into the sky, bearing the marks of their hands on its surface — the mottled face of the moon the print of the boys' fingers on the day it was freed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Stolen Fire Cast into the Sky

region.zh: 馬西姆伍德拉克島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: An old woman of Woodlark Island was sole owner of fire, while others ate raw food. Her son stole flame and gave it to mankind; in anger she divided what remained into two parts and threw them into the sky — the larger becoming the sun, the smaller the moon.
summary.zh: 伍德拉克島一老嫗獨霸火種，餘人皆食生冷。其子斥她殘忍，偷火分與眾人；老嫗怒，將所餘之火分作兩半擲上天空——大者成日，小者成月。

passages.text: The people of Woodlark Island have a tale in which the origin of the sun and moon is connected with the origin of fire. In the beginning an old woman was the sole owner of fire, and she alone could eat cooked food, while other people must devour theirs raw. Her son said to her: 'You are cruel. You see that the taro takes the skin off our throats, yet you do not give us fire with which to cook it'; but since she proved obdurate, he stole some of the flame and gave it to the rest of mankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: In anger at his action, the old woman seized what was left of her fire, divided it into two parts, and threw them into the sky, the larger portion thus becoming the sun, and the smaller the moon — the stolen fire of mankind leaving the two great lights behind in the heavens as the thief's mother's revenge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.zh: 杜杜格拉：魚父之子化為毒日

region.en: Massim district, eastern British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞東部馬西姆地區（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A woman playing with a great fish in the surf bore from a swelling on her leg a son, Dudugera. Taunted for his parentage, he was carried east by his fish-father, climbed into the sky, and as the sun nearly destroyed all things with his heat — until his mother threw lime into his face as he rose.
summary.zh: 一婦人與巨魚在海浪中嬉遊，腿上腫處迸出男嬰杜杜格拉。他因出身遭同儕辱罵，被魚父攜往東方，攀上天空化為太陽，烈炎幾滅萬物——其母登高，以石灰罐撒向初升之日，日閉目而炎減。

passages.text: A woman who was watching her garden close to the ocean, seeing a great fish sporting in the surf, walked out into the water and played with the fish, continuing to do this for several days. By and by the woman's leg, against which the fish had rubbed, began to swell and became painful until at last she got her father to make a cut in the swelling, when out popped an infant. The boy, who was named Dudugera, grew up among the other children of the village until one day, in playing a game, he threw his dart at the other children rather than at the mark, whereupon they became angry and abused him, taunting him with his parentage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fearing lest the others might really harm him, Dudugera's mother determined to send him to his father; so she took the boy to the beach, whereupon the great fish came, seized him in his mouth, and carried him far away to the east. Before he left, Dudugera warned his mother and relatives to take refuge under a great rock, for soon, he said, he would climb into a pandanus-tree and thence into the sky, and, as the sun, would destroy all things with his heat. So indeed it came to pass, for excepting his mother and her relatives, who heeded Dudugera's advice, nearly everything perished. To prevent their total annihilation his mother took a lime-calabash, and climbing upon a hill near which the sun rose, cast the lime into his face as he came up, which caused the sun to shut his eyes and thus to decrease the amount of heat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Daylight was perpetual until Qat sailed to buy night from Night himself at Vava in the Torres Islands, blackened eyebrows, sleep, and the dawn. He released it on his terrified brothers and cut it with red obsidian at cockcrow — so night became short, as it now is.
summary.zh: 白晝本永無盡頭。卡特聞托雷斯群島之瓦瓦有夜，遂買夜而歸，並學得睡意、黎明與晨鳥。他對驚恐的兄弟們釋出黑夜，教他們閉眼而眠；雞鳥報曉之際，以紅色黑曜石割開黑夜——於是夜短如今日。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-creation (Codrington telling of buying the night).

passages.text: In the Banks Islands, after Qat had formed men, pigs, trees, and rocks, he still did not know how to make night, for daylight was continuous. His brothers said to him, 'This is not at all pleasant. Here is nothing but day. Can't you do something for us?' Now Qat heard that at Vava in the Torres Islands there was night, so he took a pig, and went to Vava, where he bought night from I-Qong, Night, who lived there. Other accounts say that Qat sailed to the edge of the sky to buy night from Night, who blackened his eyebrows, showed him sleep and taught him how to make the dawn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: Qat returned to his brothers, bringing a fowl and other birds to give notice of the dawn. He begged his brothers to prepare beds of coco-nut fronds. Then for the first time, they saw the sun sinking in the west, and they cried out to Qat that it was crawling away. 'It will soon be gone,' said he, 'and if you see a change on the face of the earth, that is night.' Then he let go the night. 'What is this coming out of the sea,' they cried, 'and covering the sky?' 'That is night,' said he, 'sit down on both sides of the house, and when you feel something in your eyes, lie down and be quiet.' Presently it was dark, and their eyes began to blink. 'Qat! Qat! what is this? Shall we die?' 'Shut your eyes,' said he, 'that is it, go to sleep.' When night had lasted long enough the cock began to crow and the birds to twitter; Qat took a piece of red obsidian and cut the night with it; the light over which the night had spread itself shone forth again, and Qat's brothers awoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dog That Swam for Fire

region.zh: 莫爾茲比港莫圖村落（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The ancestors of the Motu ate raw food until smoke was seen rising from a far island. Snake, bandicoot, bird, and kangaroo all tried and failed to cross the sea; only the dog swam out, seized a blazing brand from the cooking women, and brought fire home to all the people.
summary.zh: 莫圖人先祖無火，日晒煮食。一日見遠島升起炊煙，蛇、袋狸、鳥、袋鼠相繼渡海取火，皆因浪大而返；唯犬游至島上，見婦女炊食，奪一支燃薪，游泳而歸，將火分與眾人。

passages.text: According to a version told by the Motu, the ancestors of the present people had no fire, and ate their food raw or cooked it in the sun until one day they perceived smoke rising out at sea. A dog, a snake, a bandicoot, a bird, and a kangaroo all saw this smoke and asked, 'Who will go to get fire?' First the snake said that he would make the attempt, but the sea was too rough, and he was compelled to come back. Then the bandicoot went, but he, too, had to return. One after another, all tried but the dog, and all were unsuccessful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the dog started and swam and swam until he reached the island whence the smoke rose. There he saw women cooking with fire, and seizing a blazing brand, he ran to the shore and swam safely back with it to the mainland, where he gave it to all the people — the first hearth of the Motu villages lit by a dog's swim through the open sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Goga's Body-Fire and the Snake That Saved It
title.zh: 葛嘎之體火與護火之蛇

region.en: Massim district, eastern British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞東部馬西姆地區（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The old woman Goga kept fire hidden in her own body and cooked for herself while ten youths ate sun-warmed food. The youngest spied her secret, stole the firebrand, and leapt a felled tree to escape; when her rain quenched all flame, fire survived only in a snake's burning tail — and the trees of the firebrands became totems.
summary.zh: 老嫗葛嘎藏火於己身，自煮自食，十名少年只得以日晒暖食。最幼者窺得其密，奪火把而逃，躍過倒木擺脫追趕；火把燙手落地，燒著枯草與露兜樹。老嫗降雨欲滅火，唯樹洞中蛇尾如炬未熄。雨停，眾少年拔蛇而取其燃尾，堆柴引火，各村聞訊來取火種——各氏族取薪之樹，遂成其圖騰。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Massim heritage. Includes local totem aition.

passages.text: Among the Massim tribes of eastern British New Guinea, people had no fire in the beginning, but simply warmed and dried their food in the sun. There was, however, a certain old woman called Goga who thus prepared food for ten of the youths, but for herself she cooked food with fire, which she obtained from her own body. Before the boys came home each day, she cleared away all traces of the fire and every scrap of cooked food, lest they should know her secret; but one day a piece of boiled taro accidentally got among the lads' food, and when the youngest ate it, he found it much better than what was usually given him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The youths resolved to discover the secret; the youngest hid and saw the old woman take the fire from her body and cook with it. They cut down a huge tree over which all tried to jump, but only the youngest succeeded, so they selected him to steal the fire. Creeping back to the house, he seized the firebrand when the old woman was not looking, and ran off with it; she chased him, but he jumped over the tree, which she was unable to do. As he ran, the brand burned his hand and he dropped it in the dry grass, which caught the blaze and set fire to a pandanus-tree near.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now, in a hole in this tree, lived a snake, whose tail caught fire and burned like a torch. The old woman, finding that she could not overtake the thief, caused a great rain to fall, hoping thus to quench the fire, but the snake stayed in his hole, and his tail was not extinguished. When the rain had stopped, the boys found the hole, pulled out the snake, and broke off its tail, which was still alight. Then making a great pile of wood, they set fire to it, and people from all the villages came and got flame, which they took home with them. Different folk used different kinds of wood for their firebrands, and the trees from which they took their brands became their totems.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The daughter of Ulimgau married a serpent who spoke with a man's voice. Their children ate raw fish until the serpent father sent the boy into his own belly to fetch fire and teach his sister to cook — the beginning of cooked food among mankind.
summary.zh: 烏林皋之女嫁與一條口吐人言之蛇。所生兒女以日光烤魚，食之猶生。蛇父令子鑽入己腹取火，交與其妹；二人以火炊魚——人間炊食自此而始。

passages.text: A version from the Admiralty Islands runs as follows. The daughter of Ulimgau went into the forest. The serpent saw her, and said, 'Come!' and the woman replied, 'Who would have you for a husband? You are a serpent. I will not marry you.' But he replied, 'My body is indeed that of a serpent, but my speech is that of a man. Come!' And the woman went and married him, and after a time she bore a boy and a girl, and her serpent husband put her away, saying, 'Go, I will take care of them and give them food.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the serpent fed the children and they grew. One day they were hungry, and he told them to catch fish and cook them; but they replied, 'The sun has not yet risen,' and by and by they ate the fish still raw and bloody. Then the serpent said to them, 'You two are spirits, for you eat your food raw. Perhaps you will eat me. You, girl, stay; and you, boy, crawl into my belly.' The boy was afraid, but his father said 'Go,' and he crept into the serpent's belly, took the fire, and brought it out to his sister. And the boy and girl lit a fire and cooked the food, and when they had eaten, the serpent asked, 'Is my kind of food or your kind of food the better?' And they answered, 'Your food is good, ours is bad.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Emakong and the Village Under the Water

region.en: Sulka country, northern New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛北部蘇爾卡人之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Diving for a lost ornament, Emakong found a village at the bottom of the stream whose people turned into snakes to sleep and owned fire, night, crickets, and the dawn-birds. He returned bearing them all, and taught the Sulka their use — though the people first fled in terror from the crackling flame.
summary.zh: 蘇爾卡人埃馬孔潛水尋找失落飾物，竟至溪底一村，村中人夜化為蛇而眠，有火、有夜、有蟋蟀與報曉之鳥。同名者贈其夜、火、蟋蟀與晨鳥之包，他攜之升水而歸；眾人見火而逃，他追告其用途，人間始有火與夜。

passages.text: There was once a time when the Sulka were ignorant of fire; but one day a man named Emakong lost one of his ornaments, which fell into a stream. Taking off his loin-cloth, he jumped in and dove to recover the lost object, but was amazed, on reaching the bottom, to find himself in the yard of a house. Many people came up and asked him his name, and when he replied that he was called Emakong, one of them said, 'Oh, that is also my name,' whereupon he took the bewildered man to his house and gave him a new loin-cloth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Great was Emakong's astonishment to see a fire in the house. At first he was afraid of it, but after he had been given cooked food and had found this much better than the raw viands which he had always eaten before, he lost his fear of the new thing. When it became night, the crickets began to sing, and his terror grew still greater when he heard resounding claps of thunder from every side and saw all the people turn into snakes in order to sleep. His namesake reassured him, saying that this was their custom, and that when day came again all would return to their human form. Then, with a loud report, he also changed into a snake, and Emakong alone retained the shape of man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the morning, when the birds sang to announce the coming day, he awoke, and with a crash all the serpents again turned into men. His namesake now did up a package for him, containing night, some fire, some crickets, and the birds that sing at dawn, and with this Emakong left, rising through the water. On reaching the shore, he threw the fire into dry grass, but when the people saw the blaze and heard the crackling of the flame, they were greatly alarmed and all fled. Emakong, however, ran after them and, telling them of his adventures, explained to them the use of the things that he had brought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Gods Debate the Death of Man
title.zh: 二神議死：蛻皮抑或埋葬

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島安布里姆島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: After man was made, the good deity proposed that old men be flayed like eels so that a new skin would grow and they would renew their youth like snakes. The malicious deity answered that they must be buried in the ground — and because the one who has the last word prevails, death came into the world.
summary.zh: 人造成之後，善神說：老人皮皺則如剝鱔般剝其皮，新皮自生，人可如蛇蛻皮而不死。惡神卻道：老則掘坑埋之。因『末語者勝』，死亡遂入人間。

passages.text: According to the version current in Ambrym, the good and the malicious deities were discussing man after he had been made. The former said: 'Our men seem to get on well, but haven't you noticed that their skins have begun to wrinkle? They are yet young, but when they are old, they will be very ugly. So when that happens, we will flay them like an eel, and a new skin will grow, and thus men shall renew their youth like the snakes and so be immortal.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the evil deity replied: 'No, it shall not be that way. When a man is old and ugly, we will dig a hole in the ground and put the body in it, and thus it shall always be among his descendants.' And because the one who has the last word prevails, death came into the world — a grave-rule set by the malice of the speaker who closed the debate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Skin That Floated Away

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Men once cast their skins like snakes and crabs and so never died. An old woman who shed hers in a stream went unrecognized by her own child; to quiet its crying she put the old skin on again — and from that time men ceased to renew their youth and died when they grew old.
summary.zh: 太初之人如蛇蟹蛻皮，蛻而復少，永不死。一老嫗於溪中蛻皮，新顏返家，其子不識，啼哭不止；她為哄幼兒，重回溪邊取回舊皮穿上——自此人不再蛻皮，老而至死。

passages.text: In the Banks Islands it is said that in the beginning men did not die, but cast their skins like snakes and crabs, and thus renewed their youth. One day an old woman went to a stream to change her skin and threw the old one into the water where, as it floated away, it caught upon a stick. When she went home, her child refused to recognize her in her new and youthful form, and to pacify the infant, who cried without ceasing, she returned and got her old skin, and put it on again. From that time men have ceased to cast their skins and have died when they grew old — mortality entangled by a mother's tenderness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Qat Summons Mate, and Tagaro the Foolish Watches the Wrong Path
title.zh: 卡特召馬特；愚塔加羅守錯路

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Because property stuck forever in the same hands, Qat summoned a man called Mate — 'Death' — laid him on a board, and held a funeral feast. Tagaro the Foolish, sent to watch the parting of the ways at Panoi, sat before the wrong path, and Mate went down to the lower world; all men have followed him since.
summary.zh: 太初人不死，惟財產永歸一手，紛擾不堪。卡特遂召一名『馬特』（死）之人，置於板上覆蓋，殺豬分其財產，舉行喪宴。第五日吹螺驅魂，啟板視之，馬特已去，僅餘白骨。卡特派愚塔加羅守帕諾伊岔路口，防馬特下界；愚者卻坐在上界之路口，馬特遂下冥府——世人從此皆循其路。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref funeral-feast aition.

passages.text: In the Banks Islands it is said that in the beginning men lived forever, casting their skins, and that the permanence of property in the same hands led to much trouble. Qat, therefore, summoned a man called Mate ('Death') and laid him on a board and covered him over; after which he killed a pig and divided Mate's property among his descendants, all of whom came and ate of the funeral feast. On the fifth day, when the conch-shells were blown to drive away the ghost, Qat removed the covering, and Mate was gone; only his bones were left.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: Meanwhile Qat had sent Tagaro the Foolish to watch the way to Panoi, where the paths to the underworld and the upper regions divide, to see that Mate did not go below; but the Fool sat before the way of the world above so that Mate descended to the lower realms; and ever since that time all men have followed Mate along the path he took.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun Calls All Things to Live Forever
title.zh: 日召萬物得不死，獨人不至

region.en: Baining country, Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島拜寧人之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: The sun called all things together and asked which wished to live forever. All came except man; so the stones and the snakes live forever, but man must die — for had he obeyed the sun's summons, he too might have changed his skin like the snake.
summary.zh: 一日召集萬物，問誰願永生。萬物皆至，唯人不至；故石與蛇長存，人則必死——若人應召，本可如蛇蛻皮而得永生。

passages.text: Thus the Baining in New Britain say that one day the sun called all things together and asked which wished to live forever. All came except man; so the stones and the snakes live forever, but man must die. Had man obeyed the sun, he would have been able to change his skin from time to time like the snake, and so would have acquired immortality — the missing summons the one missed appointment that set the human lot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

region.en: Admiralty Islands, Papua New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿德米羅提群島，巴布亞新幾內亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: Fleeing an evil spirit, a man hid in a tree that opened and closed for him; the tree asked two white pigs as payment. He brought only one true white pig and another blackened with chalk — and the tree revoked its shelter, dooming the race to mortality and the enmity of evil spirits.
summary.zh: 一人遭惡靈追殺，大樹開合庇之；樹索白豬二頭為酬。此人以白垩塗黑豬充數，樹責其忘恩：『若你誠實，遇險皆可入我身避之；如今不能，你必死。』人類之必死與惡靈之仇，皆由此不誠而起。

passages.text: A man once went out fishing; but since an evil spirit wished to kill and eat him, he fled into the forest. There he caused a tree to open, and creeping inside, the tree closed again, so that when the evil being came, he did not see his victim and went away, whereupon the tree opened, and the man came out. The tree said to him, 'Bring to me two white pigs.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the man went to his village and got two pigs, but he cheated the tree in that he brought only a single white one, the other being black whitened with chalk. For this the tree rebuked him and said: 'You are unthankful, though I was good to you. If you had done what I had asked, you might have taken refuge in me whenever danger threatened. Now you cannot, but must die.' So, as a result of this man's ingratitude, the human race is doomed to mortality and cannot escape the enmity of evil spirits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

region.en: Southern British New Guinea coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞南部海岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A great flood overflowed the hills of British New Guinea; people and animals fled to the peak of Tauaga. Only the serpent-king Raudalo did not fear: he touched the angry waters with his forked tongue, and the sea turned and flowed back down the mountain to its bed.
summary.zh: 洪水暴發，海沒群山，人畜奔逃至最高峰陶阿加。唯蛇王勞達洛不懼，屢問僕蛇水勢，終以舌端觸水，海水頓止而退；蛇王更追洪下山，以舌驅之，直至海復其位，洪水乃平。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); coastal PNG heritage. Cross-tradition flood cluster.

passages.text: Once a great flood occurred, and the sea rose and overflowed the earth, the hills being covered, and people and animals hurrying to the top of Tauaga, the highest mountain. But the sea followed and all were afraid. Yet the king of the snakes, Raudalo, did not fear. At last he said to his servants, 'Where now are the waters?' And they answered, 'They are rising, lord.' Yet looked he not upon the flood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: And after a space he said again, 'Where now are the waters?' and his servants answered as they had done before. And again he inquired of them, 'Where now are the waters?' But this time all the snakes, Titiko, Dubo and Anaur, made answer, 'They are here, and in a moment they will touch thee, lord.' Then Raudalo turned him about and put forth his forked tongue, and touched with the tip of it the angry waters which were about to cover him. And on a sudden the sea rose no more, but began to flow down the side of the mountain. Still was Raudalo not content, and he pursued the flood down the hill, ever and anon putting forth his forked tongue that there might be no tarrying on the way. Thus went they down the mountain and over the plain country until the sea shore was reached, and the waters lay in their bed once more and the flood was stayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Abaia the Lake Eel Drowns the Village

region.en: British New Guinea lake country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞湖區（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. I

summary.en: A village plundered the fish of a lake whose depths held the magic eel Abaia. When a woman even laid hold of the great eel, he raised a night of rain; the lake rose and drowned them all save one old woman who had not eaten of the fish and saved herself in a tree.
summary.zh: 村民捕盡一湖之魚，湖底潛有神鰻阿拜亞。一婦人竟捉住大鰻，鰻怒而興連夜大雨，湖水暴漲，村人盡沒；唯未食魚之一老嫗攀樹得生。

passages.text: One day a man discovered a lake in which were many fish; and at the bottom of the lake lived a magic eel, but the man knew it not. He caught many fish and returned the next day with the people of his village whom he had told of his discovery; and they also were very successful, while one woman even laid hold of the great eel, Abaia, who dwelt in the depths of the lake, though he escaped her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now Abaia was angry that his fish had been caught and that he himself had been seized, so he caused a great rain to fall that night, and the waters of the lake also rose, and all the people were drowned except an old woman who had not eaten of the fish and who saved herself in a tree. The old eel's deluge spared only her who had kept the taboo of the lake's abundance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. I (1916); not verbatim.
